decisions.quote: We conducted two studies to test the effect of repeated flexion finger movements on approach motivation. The results of the two studies were inconsistent with each other as well as with the original Haeffel ( 2011 ) study (see Figure 1 ).
decisions.reason: The authors conclude that neither Study 1 (direct replication) nor Study 2 (conceptual replication) replicated the original Haeffel (2011) findings (which were gender-moderated effects on the BAS-Fun subscale and persistence on the difficult anagram task). Although each study yielded an isolated statistically significant main effect on a different variable (positive affect in Study 1; total BAS in Study 2) where the original found none, the authors explicitly judge the two studies inconsistent with the original study, argue that the isolated significant results are likely chance false positives that do not survive multiple-comparison correction, Suspect the original 2011 interaction was a false positive, and conclude that their findings align with non-replications in psychology.
